content:
Introduction

The vanilla taktx-client contains all the functionality to communicate with the TaktX plaform. It allows you to deploy process definitions, start process instances, send messages and signals and even allows you to subscribe to the InstanceUpdateRecord stream to get deep insight into what happened with your flows. 

Maven/gradle dependency

To start using it in a Java based application you need to add a gradle/maven dependency to the specific version of the taktx-client which is compatible with your TaktX platform. 

When using maven: 

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.taktx</groupId>
    <artifactId>taktx-client</artifactId>
    <version>0.4.0-beta-1</version>
</dependency>

When using gradle:

implementation("io.taktx:taktx-client:0.4.0-beta-1")

This will make sure the taktx-client and all transitive dependencies are included into your application. 

Creating the client object

To create the client object a TaktClientBuilder has been introduced. Create an instance of the TaktXClient with the following:

Properties taktProperties = new Properties();
TaktXClientBuilder taktClientBuilder = TaktXClient.newClientBuilder();
taktClient = taktClientBuilder.withTaktProperties(taktProperties).build();
taktClient.start();

The taktProperties will have to be filled with the correct configuration parameters. This should at least include the following properties. Enter the property values for your environment.

bootstrap.servers=localhost:9092
taktx.engine.namespace=namespace

There a lots more configuration parameters. See the Client Configuration section for the details.

There are two ways on how to use the TaktXClient, first one is purely calling public API. The second one is by leveraging the power of annotations. 

Using the public API

Once the TaktXClient has been started, you can use the public API to deploy process definitions, start process instances, send messages and signals and even subscribe to the event stream. For the full javadoc look here and look at github at the client-worker-vanilla-pure for an example implementation.

Deploying BPMN files

Registering a jobworker

Create class which implements the io.taktx.client.ExternalTaskTriggerConsumer interface. It will need to implement two methods:

  • The getJobIds method should return the task-ids that this worker will support

  • The acceptBatch method which will need to support all external task requests 

Using Annotations

As described in the paragraphs above, you see that especially the worker implementation is a bit cumbersome. The client does provide an alternative and easier way to deploy BPMN resources and create and manage workers. This way the classpath is scanned for specific annotations and the client will make sure the correct wiring is in place. Look at github at the client-worker-vanilla-annotions for an example implementation.

Deploying BPMN files

To automatically deploy BPMN files we need to add the @Deployment annotation. For example on the main class or on a Configuration bean. 

By calling  deployTaktDeploymentAnnotatedClasses on the TaktXClient all @Deployment annotations will be scanned and all corresponding BPMN files will be deployed automatically.

Starting workers

By registering the AnnotationScanningExternalTaskTriggerConsumer as externalTaskTriggerConsumer we can also scan the codebase automatically for @TaktWorkerMethod annotations and do all wiring automatically.



The worker classes must have a default constructor so they can be instantiated by the PlainJavaInstanceProvider(). After that each worker method can be annotated by the JobWorker annotation and the variables and response will be mapped to/from in-engine variables automatically
